{{< include _poly-kit.qmd >}}

In much music of West and Central Africa, a drum ensemble is built from several short parts that repeat,
each fitting the same cycle in its own way. No part is "the" rhythm: the music is the way they lock together.
The Ewe people of Ghana and Togo are the example most often studied, and this page uses an Ewe-style texture.
It is a simplified model for practice, not a transcription of a particular piece.

## The cycle: twelve pulses

Many of these pieces run on a cycle of twelve fast pulses. Twelve divides by 2, 3, 4 and 6, so it holds
four beats of three *and* three beats of four at once. That is why the music can feel like 12/8 and 3/4 at
the same time.

<div class="poly" data-layers="4;3" data-names="Four beats (feet);Three beats" data-sounds="kick;wood" data-bpm="60" data-beat="0"></div>

Dancers often step the four beats. Listen to the four, then let the three pull against it.

## The bell pattern

The part that holds the ensemble together is usually an iron bell (in Ewe music the double bell
*gankogui*). Its most widespread pattern is seven strokes in twelve pulses, often called the
**standard pattern**:

`x . x . x x . x . x . x`

<div class="poly" data-layers="x.x.xx.x.x.x;4" data-names="Bell;Four beats" data-sounds="bell;kick" data-bpm="60" data-beat="1"></div>

The pattern is uneven on purpose: long and short gaps (2 2 1 2 2 2 1). Players and listeners use it as the
reference for where every other part goes, the way a jazz drummer's ride cymbal works.

**Try it.** Mute the bell and clap it against the four beats. Then mute the beats and step them while the bell
plays.

## Layering the ensemble

Add parts one at a time: the bell, a shaker on every pulse with an accent each beat, a low drum on the four,
and a high drum playing three.

<div class="poly" data-layers="x.x.xx.x.x.x;X..X..X..X..;4;3" data-names="Bell;Shaker;Low drum (4);High drum (3)" data-sounds="bell;shaker;kick;hi" data-bpm="60" data-beat="2"></div>

Mute layers in turn. With only the bell and the three, the music seems to be in three; with the bell and the
four, in four. With all of them it is both.

## Hearing it from the inside

A useful exercise from many teachers: keep the four beats with your feet, clap the bell, and say the three.
Start very slowly. When it feels stable, change which part you clap. The goal is to hear each part as a
line in its own right, not as an off-beat of something else.

## Unverified, to check

The facts on this page are from memory and have not yet been checked against a source: the name
*gankogui*, the term "standard pattern" (usually credited to A. M. Jones), and the dancers' four-beat step.
They are listed in the sources file as unverified.
